title: Casper and the Well
premise: Silas Joubert arrives in the drowned-hollow village of Casper's Well to teach at a school where children vanish one desk at a time, always on the night the melted bell rings. The villagers survive by never being chosen: they feed the well a name each generation, and this year the well has grown tired of children and wants the teacher. To end it, Silas must learn the bell-song's forbidden last verse from the village's oldest living woman—without ever singing along—while falling for the constable sworn to keep the tradition intact. In the end Silas sings the last verse alone, giving the well a name that was never the village's to give: their own, traded for the children's return and a silence that costs them their reflection, their past, and the love they finally admitted to.
about_author: Silas Galloway spent a decade teaching in remote coastal villages before turning to horror, drawing on the folk songs and half-buried church records of places that prefer to be forgotten. They live alone, deliberately, near a dry well they have never once looked into.

chapters.title: The Long Road Down
chapters.summary: Silas's third-person POV opens the drive into Casper's Well, a village sunk in a hollow with no cell signal and too many shutters. The schoolhouse is half-empty; the headmaster's ledger shows enrollment dropping by one child each autumn. Emotional beat: uneasy charm, the sense of a place performing normalcy.

chapters.title: Twenty-Six Desks, Nineteen Children
chapters.summary: Silas teaches their first week, counting seats that stay cold. A girl, Maren, draws a bell with no clapper on every worksheet. The constable, Edith Vane, visits to 'welcome' Silas and warn them against walking after dark. POV Silas. Beat: curiosity curdling into wrongness.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Silas digs through school records at night and finds decades of missing children, each file ending mid-sentence, each dated to the same week in November. The oldest entry mentions a bell 'given to the water.' Beat: the thrill of investigation turning to dread.

chapters.title: Edith
chapters.summary: A quieter chapter from Silas's POV: Edith walks them home, shares bread, laughs at their skepticism, and something real sparks between them—cut short when Edith sees Silas's lantern and goes pale. Beat: warmth with a fault line running under it.

chapters.title: The Bell That Was Melted
chapters.summary: Silas confirms in parish records the bell was melted in 1911, its metal sold. That night, at 3 a.m., the bell rings—one clear note that rattles their teeth. Every villager's shutters close at once. Beat: belief knocked loose, not converted.

chapters.title: Nineteen, Eighteen
chapters.summary: Maren's desk is empty. No absence note, no search, no grief—the class simply moves her chair away. Edith refuses to discuss it, and Silas sees the well's rim for the first time, ringed with small shoes. Beat: horror becomes intimate.

chapters.title: The Song
chapters.summary: Silas hears the children humming a tune none will name, always stopping at the same bar. The school cook, old Bram, hums the third verse drunk and weeps. Silas records it; the recording plays a fourth verse Silas didn't capture. Beat: the mystery gains a voice.

chapters.title: Grandmother Ilsa
chapters.summary: Silas seeks out Ilsa Kettering, ninety-one, the last person taught the song entire. She refuses to speak the last verse, but tells them the well takes a name each generation and the village chooses whose. Beat: the horror's mechanics revealed—survival has always been a transaction.

chapters.title: Rules of Staying Invisible
chapters.summary: Edith, cornered, explains the covenant: never sing along, never answer the bell, never be the name. She was raised to enforce it and hates it. Silas and Edith's bond deepens into something confessed at 2 a.m. Beat: love against duty, made explicit.

chapters.title: The Well Wants a Teacher
chapters.summary: The bell rings two nights running. Silas's name appears scratched inside the school ledger in handwriting matching their own. Villagers begin avoiding eye contact, then avoiding the street. Beat: the protagonist realizes they are already chosen.

chapters.title: Maren's Voice
chapters.summary: Silas hears Maren singing from the well at night, voice unchanged since she vanished. Following it, they nearly answer the bell-song's call and are dragged back by Edith, who burns her hand on the well's rope to do it. Beat: guilt, and the cost of Edith's duty.

chapters.title: The Fourth Verse
chapters.summary: Ilsa, dying, agrees to teach Silas the last verse on one condition: hear it, never sing it. The verse is a naming—a way to give the well a name of one's own choosing instead of the village's. Beat: hope arrives with a terrible price tag.

chapters.title: The Village Votes
chapters.summary: Silas discovers the elders have already decided: the well will take the teacher, ending a century of losing children. Even kind Bram voted yes. Silas flees to Edith, who must choose between her oath and them. Beat: betrayal; the theme of survival's price turns on the village itself.

chapters.title: Edith's Choice
chapters.summary: Edith burns the covenant book, an act that unmakes her family's standing and her own name in the village rolls—literally; her name fades from every record. She chooses Silas. Beat: love against duty, duty losing, at cost.

chapters.title: The Ringing Week
chapters.summary: The bell rings nightly now; the water rises in the hollow; the well's rim widens toward the school. Children hum the song in their sleep. Silas rehearses the last verse silently, mouthing it, terrified of a single sounded note. Beat: rising dread, the clock audible in every chapter break.

chapters.title: What Ilsa Kept
chapters.summary: Ilsa dies, and among her papers Silas finds the truth: the 1911 bell was melted to stop the song, and it failed because the well doesn't need the bell—it needs a singer. The ringing is a summons, and Silas has been hearing their own voice reflected back. Beat: the horror inverts; the enemy is the protagonist's own throat.

chapters.title: Nineteen Again
chapters.summary: The missing children return at dawn, standing wet at the schoolhouse door, alive but singing in unison, waiting. The village rejoices and recoils. Maren tells Silas: 'He's saving you a seat.' Beat: relief poisoned; the stakes sharpen.

chapters.title: The Seat
chapters.summary: Silas visits the well in daylight, sees the nineteenth desk at the water's bottom, their name carved in the wood. They understand: singing the last verse names the taker, but the singer must stand where it can reach. Edith begs them to run. Beat: the choice crystallizes.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: At midnight of the ringing week, Silas stands at the well and sings the final verse alone—naming the well with their own full name, offering themselves in exchange for the children's release. The bell rings one last time. Beat: climax; sacrifice chosen, not taken.

chapters.title: The Water Takes Its Due
chapters.summary: The well accepts. The children wake from the song, whole. Silas is pulled down singing, and Edith, bound by her new oath to the village, holds the rope until it goes slack. Beat: grief and awe; the price fully paid.

chapters.title: After the Silence
chapters.summary: Spring. The school has all its children; Maren keeps a desk empty in the corner and no one questions it. The bell never rings again. Edith teaches part-time and keeps Silas's name alive where the ledgers erased it. Beat: mourning braided with peace.

chapters.title: Coda: The New Teacher
chapters.summary: Years later, a new teacher arrives and finds a class of twenty-six desks and twenty-six children—too many, never too few. On the last page, someone has chalked the first three bars of a song on the board, unfinished. Beat: the cycle broken, or merely patient; the horror exhales.
